- If sentiment is negative or near-zero in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or shift downward.
- If sentiment is positive and prices are trending up, model often overshoots early in the horizon; cap upward momentum after 3–5 days.
- When true prices show sharp downward spikes (e.g., >10% drop from prior day), model fails to adjust; add a downward correction buffer if sentiment is neutral or negative.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true price drops sharply, model is lagging; apply a “mean reversion” rule: if 3-day average of true prices is below forecast, reduce forecast by 1–2% per day.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is positive and model is rising steadily, check for “overconfidence bias” — if forecast exceeds 10% above recent 7-day high, reduce by 5–10%.
- If sentiment is positive but true price is volatile or erratic, model tends to smooth too much — allow for 1–2% volatility buffer in forecast.
- If sentiment is negative and model is rising, consider “sentiment reversal” — if sentiment turns positive within 3 days, reduce forecast by 2–5% to avoid overcorrection.
